slides.say: A B C is an isosceles triangle, with A B equal to A C, and angle B A C is four theta degrees, where theta is between zero and forty-five. B lies on a circle with center O and radius r. A B and B C meet the circle again at D and E. What is the length of the arc D E that does not contain B?
at: A B C is an isosceles triangle

slides.say: There are letters everywhere, so we'll solve it in two different ways, the math way, and then by plugging in numbers. [short pause] Let's start with the math way. We need an arc length, and for that we first need a central angle.
at: Let's start with the math way

slides.say: Look at the isosceles triangle first. A B is equal to A C, so angle B is equal to angle C. The angles of a triangle add up to a hundred eighty, so together they're a hundred eighty minus four theta. They're equal, so each one is half of that. Half of a hundred eighty is ninety, and half of four theta is two theta. So each base angle is ninety minus two theta.
at: so angle B is equal to angle C
so angle B is equal to angle C

slides.say: The arc we need is on the circle near B, whose center is O. So let's take this part of the figure and look at it bigger.
at: The arc we need is on the circle

slides.say: Here's the circle near B, bigger. Angle B is still ninety minus two theta. Its sides go through D and E, so it's an inscribed angle in the circle, and it stands on the bold arc D E. The central angle on the same arc is twice as big.
at: Its sides go through D and E

slides.say: So let's draw the radii O D and O E. The central angle is two times, ninety minus two theta. Two times ninety is a hundred eighty, and two times two theta is four theta. So the central angle is a hundred eighty minus four theta.
at: draw the radii O D and O E
The central angle is two times
So the central angle is a hundred eighty

slides: Did you notice? We divided by two, and then we multiplied by two. If you see that early, you can write a hundred eighty minus four theta right away.

slides.say: An arc is the part of the circumference set by the central angle, out of three hundred sixty. So the arc is a hundred eighty minus four theta, over three hundred sixty, times two pi r.

There are many letters, so let's glance at the choices and work toward them. Every choice has pi r, and we have two pi r. So we cancel the two with the three hundred sixty, and we're left with a hundred eighty at the bottom, times pi r.

Every choice also has a one in the bracket. So we split our fraction into two fractions with the same bottom, a hundred eighty over a hundred eighty, minus four theta over a hundred eighty. Why is that allowed? Two fractions with the same bottom are subtracted by subtracting the tops, so we can also go back the other way.

A hundred eighty over a hundred eighty is one. And four over a hundred eighty is one over forty-five, because a hundred eighty divided by four is forty-five. So the arc is pi r, times the bracket one minus theta over forty-five. Choice number four is our answer.
at: So the arc is pi r
Choice number four is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's use plugging in numbers. The right choice must be true for every theta and every r that the question allows. So it must also be true for one example that we choose. We pick easy numbers, find the arc, and then put the same numbers in the choices.
at: Now let's use plugging in numbers

slides.say: Which example is the easiest? An equilateral triangle, with all its angles sixty degrees. Here it is, in its own picture. Then four theta is sixty, so theta is sixty divided by four, fifteen. That's between zero and forty-five, so it's allowed.
at: Here it is, in its own picture
so theta is sixty divided by four

slides.say: So angle B is sixty, and the central angle on the bold arc is twice as big, a hundred twenty. The radius isn't given either, so let's take r as one, an easy number.
at: the central angle on the bold arc
twice as big, a hundred twenty

slides.say: The whole circumference is two pi times one, two pi. A hundred twenty out of three hundred sixty is one third. So the arc is a third of two pi, two pi over three.
at: So the arc is a third

slides.say: Now we put theta fifteen and r one in every choice, and cross out any choice that doesn't give two pi over three. If one fits early, we still check the others, because an example can fit more than one choice.
Choice number one says pi r, times one minus theta over fifteen. Fifteen over fifteen is one, and one minus one is zero. Zero, not two pi over three, so it's out.
Choice number two says pi r, times one minus theta over thirty. Fifteen over thirty is a half, and one minus a half is a half. That gives pi over two, not two pi over three, so it's out.
Choice number three says pi r, times one minus theta over ninety. Fifteen over ninety is a sixth, and one minus a sixth is five sixths. Five pi over six, not two pi over three, so it's out.

Now the other three are out, so choice number four is the only one left. Let's still check it. Choice number four says pi r, times one minus theta over forty-five. Fifteen over forty-five is a third, and one minus a third is two thirds. Two pi over three, it fits. Choice number four is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number four is our answer
